newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-GBL's Suez stake buy seen heralding big move.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-GBL's Suez stake buy seen heralding big move.

text.p: Belgian financier Albert Frere snapped up five million shares in French Compagnie de Suez on Monday, leaving analysts pondering his next big move.
"Frere never buys anything without a reason," Brussels-based KB Securities analyst Dirk Peeters told Reuters. "But for now it's impossible to predict what he is planning."

Belgian holding company Electrafina, a unit of Frere's Groupe Bruxelles Lambert (GBL), said it would pay French oil group Elf Aquitaine about six billion Belgian francs ($190 million) for the 2.9 percent stake. Elf declined to comment.
"We are taking the stake with Suez's blessing," Electrafina chief executive officer Thierry de Rudder said.

"The Suez acquisition was an opportunity which presented itself. It is a good financial investment. It also shows our good understanding with the chief executive officer of Suez (Gerard Mestrallet)," he added.

The move took analysts by surprise, coming less than a month after the GBL group severed one of its last remaining links with Suez, selling 24 percent of Belgian utility Tractebel to Suez unit Societe Generale de Belgique.
Many had expected that Electrafina would reinvest some of the 41 billion Belgian francs it got from the deal in Luxembourg broadcaster Cie Luxembourgeoise de Telediffusion (CLT).
Electrafina controls CLT via Luxembourg holding company Audiofina.

"They have to do something with this money. When they sell something like Tractebel that has given them so much solid dividend income they have to find something to replace it," Generale Bank analyst Luc Van der Elst said.
"It may be that GBL and Frere are just putting out some links with other groups to get them involved in a bigger transaction," Peeters said.
Elf's sale was less surprising, being just the latest in a planned 10 billion French franc programme of divestments.

This year Elf has already sold its interests in Belgian oil group Petrofina (also controlled by Electrafina) and, last Thursday, sold its entire 7.06 percent stake in Belgium's Compagnie Nationale a Portefeuille/Nationale Portefeuillemaatschapij (CNP/NPM), another company in Frere's business empire.

Suez's Mestrallet has also made no secret that he wants to unwind the cross shareholdings that were built up between Suez, SGB and Elf at the time the French oil group was privatized in 1994. SGB has said separately that its own small stakes in Elf and Suez are also up for sale.
But analysts did not think that Frere had bought into Suez just to help it fulfill this goal.
"I do not think it's the ultimate goal. You cannot say this is only done to do away with the cross-links that exist. It does not seem to be the big strategy," Van der Elst said.

Some analysts have speculated in recent months that Suez may want to simplify its group structure by merging with SGB, or -- following SGB's Tractebel buy -- overseeing Suez/SGB's merger with a French conglomerate like Compagnie Generale des Eaux.

Peeters said, however, that he did not think Frere was interested in any such strategy. "GBL and Suez are 180 degree opposites in this respect...Frere likes to use holdings to control as many companies as possible," he said.
De Rudder declined to say whether the GBL-Electrafina group planned further acquisitions of Suez stock.
